notes.meaning: The heavenly guide measured the south gate of the outer courtyard. It had windows all around to let in light, and its full size was fifty cubits long by twenty-five cubits wide, matching the other outer gates. This showed that God's house is built with perfect balance and order.

Seven steps led up from the ground outside to this southern gateway. Palm trees were carved into the pillars on both sides, just like the other gates. The steps remind worshippers that coming before God means rising above ordinary life.

Across the outer courtyard was another gate that led into the inner court. The guide measured the open space between the outer gate and the inner gate to be one hundred cubits, or about 175 feet. This wide distance gave plenty of room for worshippers while keeping the inner sacred space separate.

The guide next led Ezekiel through the southern gateway into the inner courtyard. When he measured this inner gate, he found it had the exact same size as the outer gates. God's design was completely consistent across the entire temple complex.

The guardrooms, pillars, and entry porch of this inner gate had the same measurements as the outer gates. It also had windows running all around it, measuring fifty cubits long and twenty-five cubits wide. God's house was designed with light and harmony in every part.

The entry porches around the inner court measured twenty-five cubits long and five cubits deep. Some ancient copies of the Bible do not include this sentence, and scholars debate its exact placement. Even so, it underlines the careful measuring of every part of the holy building.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Several scholars think this verse was added to the text later, because the old Greek translation leaves it out and its numbers are hard to fit.

notes.meaning: The porch of this inner south gate opened outward toward the outer court, and its pillars were decorated with carved palm trees. While the outer gates had seven steps, this inner gate had eight steps leading up to it. The extra step showed that moving closer to God required an even higher level of reverence.

The guide then brought Ezekiel around to the inner gate on the east side. He measured it and found it had the exact same dimensions as the south gate. God provided multiple entrances that were all equally prepared for sacred worship.

The east inner gate also had matching guardrooms, side pillars, and an entryway porch. It was fifty cubits long and twenty-five cubits wide, with windows all around it. The repeating design highlighted that God's standard of holiness is the same from every direction.

Like the south gate, this eastern gate had a porch facing the outer court and pillars decorated with palm trees. It also had eight steps leading up to it from the outer courtyard. Each approach to God's inner presence required the same upward climb in holiness.

The guide next took Ezekiel to the inner gate on the north side. He measured it and discovered it was built to the same dimensions as the south and east gates. Every entrance into the inner court was treated with equal care and honor.

The north gate possessed the same guardrooms, side pillars, entryway porch, and surrounding windows. Its total size was fifty cubits long by twenty-five cubits wide. Its symmetry mirrored the other gates, showing that God's plans are orderly and complete.

Its porch also faced out toward the outer courtyard, with carved palm trees on its pillars and eight steps leading up. This completed the tour of the three inner gates. The higher elevation set the inner area apart as a more sacred space for the priests.

Next to the inner gateway was a special side room with a door where the priests washed the burnt offerings. According to the law of Moses, parts of the animal had to be rinsed with water before being offered on the altar. This washing stressed that only what was clean and pure could be presented to God.

Inside the porch of the gateway were four tables, two on each side, used for preparing the sacrifices. These included the burnt offering, the sin offering to make amends for wrongdoing, and the guilt offering for specific offenses. The temple was built to handle animal sacrifices according to God's holy rules.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe these animal sacrifices will literally take place in a future millennial temple as visual memorials of Jesus' finished death on the cross.
Many evangelicals believe these sacrifices symbolically picture the spiritual worship of the church, since Jesus completely fulfilled and ended Old Testament animal sacrifices.

notes.meaning: Outside the doorway of the north gate were four more tables, two on one side of the steps and two on the other. This brought the total number of preparation tables near the gate to eight. Having tables both inside and outside gave the priests plenty of room to prepare the offerings without overcrowding.

In all, there were eight tables set around the gateway—four on the inside and four on the outside. All eight were dedicated to slaughtering and preparing the sacrificial animals. This large number made sure that the worship of God could proceed smoothly and without delay.

Near the entrance stood four more tables cut from solid stone, each about two feet square and eighteen inches high. The priests placed their knives and other slaughtering tools on these stone tables. God cared about the practical tools needed for holy worship just as much as the sacred building itself.

Double-pronged hooks, about three inches long, were attached to the walls inside the gateway area. These held the meat of the sacrifices while the priests prepared it for the altar. Every detail was arranged to keep the sacred offerings orderly and clean.

Inside the inner court, near the gateways, were two special side rooms. One room stood by the north gate facing south, and the other stood by the south gate facing north. These rooms were set aside for the priests who served in the temple courts.

The guide explained that the chamber facing south was for the priests who watched over the daily duties of the temple building. They took care of the house of God and made sure its laws and services were kept according to God's command. Their job was to protect the sanctuary from any neglect or defilement.

The chamber facing north was reserved for the priests who served at the altar of sacrifice. God assigned this holy duty specifically to the family of Zadok because they had remained loyal to the Lord when others turned away. Access to the altar was restricted to those whom God had chosen and proven faithful.

The guide then measured the inner courtyard, which was a perfect square of one hundred cubits on each side. The altar of sacrifice stood directly in the center of this court in front of the temple building. The square shape symbolized divine perfection, and the altar showed that sacrifice was at the heart of approaching God.

The guide led Ezekiel to the porch or entry hall of the temple building itself. He measured the side pillars flanking the entrance to be five cubits thick, and the gateway opening to be fourteen cubits wide. Ezekiel was now moving from the courtyard into the most sacred structure of the complex.

The temple porch was twenty cubits wide and eleven or twelve cubits deep, reached by a flight of steps. Two freestanding columns stood beside the doorway pillars, much like the famous bronze pillars outside Solomon's temple. Walking up these steps brought the worshipper to the threshold of God's dwelling place.
